extracted.intended_audience: startup founders / first-time inventors preparing provisional patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing, using, and protecting priority with U.S. provisional patent applications (12-month priority placeholder and planning tool before filing a non‑provisional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional is not a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional is not a patent: it is not examined, it cannot be enforced, it does not extend the 20-year patent term, and it does not, by itself, give you the right to mark 'patent pending' on something it does not actually disclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a provisional as an enforceable right or as equivalent to a granted patent. Understand its procedural/record-keeping role rather than as substantive protection; ensure any 'patent pending' marking is supported by the provisional's disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional as a 12-month priority-date placeholder
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional functions as a priority-date placeholder: for 12 months you can file a non‑provisional that claims priority back to the provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art that appears between the provisional and non‑provisional filing dates does not count against you, but only for subject matter that was actually disclosed in the provisional. Plan your non‑provisional filing within the 12‑month window if you want to rely on the provisional's date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority applies only to subject matter actually disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority is limited to the subject matter actually disclosed in the provisional; claims in a later non‑provisional are only entitled to the provisional date to the extent their claim elements are supported by that disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting provisional content, be explicit in disclosing every feature you might later claim; failure to disclose a claim element means losing priority for that element (and potential exposure to intervening prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat provisional disclosure like a non‑provisional specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft the provisional as if it were a non‑provisional spec: every claim element you might ever want should appear in some form in the provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include figures, alternative embodiments, numerical ranges, and the rationale for novelty. The article emphasizes 'the cost of writing a fat provisional is small compared to the cost of losing priority.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include figures, alternative embodiments, and numerical ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong provisional should include drawings, alternative embodiments, numerical ranges, and explanatory framing (e.g., 'why this is novel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete disclosures (figures and multiple embodiments) increase the likelihood that later claim elements will be supported; avoid sparse narrative-only filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Disclosure Trap: avoid filing 'thin' provisionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many provisionals are filed too thin (e.g., a short 4‑page narrative), which creates risk that later non‑provisional claims won't be supported and priority will be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern example: founder files a brief narrative provisional and later spends thousands on a non‑provisional with claims; examiner cites a reference and the new claims lack support in the provisional. Counter this by richer initial disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple provisionals allowed and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file additional provisional applications during the 12‑month window and later consolidate them into a single non‑provisional that claims priority to all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your invention evolves, file updated provisionals at milestones. Multiple provisionals are relatively cheap and can be used to capture development over the year; the non‑provisional can claim priority to each provisional that supports its subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the provisional year to test the market
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 12‑month provisional period to build prototypes, get customer feedback, learn what matters, and prepare a stronger non‑provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the year as product validation time: iterate on the invention and use empirical learning to craft a more accurate and valuable non‑provisional application rather than rushing to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 12‑month deadline is strict (the '12‑Month Cliff')
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing the 12‑month deadline by even one day causes loss of priority; there is no extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calendar the deadline in multiple places (the article suggests 'calendar it in three places') and plan filings accordingly; do not assume grace periods or extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing (Paris Convention) implications tied to the same 12‑month deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: The 12‑month provisional priority deadline is also the Paris Convention deadline for foreign filings: to secure foreign patent rights you must file PCT or national applications within that same period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want patents in Europe, Japan, China, etc., plan international/PCT or direct national filings by the 12‑month cutoff to preserve priority.
